description: I’m a  professional disaster analyst at an Indonesian government agency, specializing in data engineering and geospatial analysis. I build pipelines for satellite data with GEE and programming language, turning raw Earth observation imagery into analysis-ready datasets for rice and climate-risk mapping. I’m looking for teammates with machine learning and forecasting skills, plus a developer for dashboards or a rice agronomist. Let’s turn Earth observation data into actionable insights!
summary:
This project develops a machine learning model to predict cropping patterns and determine the optimal start of the planting season in Indonesia, specifically on the island of Java. By integrating remote sensing time-series data (NDVI and LSWI indices), IMERG satellite rainfall data, and five years of historical agricultural records, this system comprehensively addresses two key challenges: crop intensity classification (IP100 to IP300) and regression modeling to predict planting dates.
Engineered features such as vegetation amplitude, dry-season soil moisture, and the onset of rainfall are processed using Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms. This approach is crucial for supporting precision agriculture, optimizing land productivity, and mitigating the risk of crop failure due to increasingly unpredictable climate variability. The final results provide accurate and adaptive data-driven recommendations for farmers and policymakers in planning the planting season. Broadly speaking, this innovation contributes significantly to enhancing national food security through proactive, efficient, and sustainable climate adaptation strategies at the local level, while accelerating the digital transformation of Indonesia’s agricultural sector toward a more resilient Agriculture 4.0 era.
details:
Project Title: Rice Planting Calendar Monitoring and Forecasting for Purworejo, Central Java

Overview

This project builds a satellite-based system for mapping rice planting seasons in Banyuwangi Regency and for estimating when planting will start in upcoming seasons. It combines three data sources: Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery to observe crop growth, IMERG satellite rainfall to locate the start of the wet season, and ERA5 climate reanalysis to describe large-scale ocean and atmospheric conditions.

How It Works

The system runs in two stages. In the first, Google Earth Engine processes HLS imagery for each rice field polygon in the Banyuwangi asset layer. For every 15-day period from October to September, it computes the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Land Surface Water Index (LSWI), then smooths the time series by filling gaps caused by cloud cover. A peak-and-trough detection algorithm identifies growing cycles and assigns each planting date to a main season (MT1, MT2, or MT3). It also flags flooding periods using a combination of low NDVI and high LSWI, and classifies each polygon by cropping intensity (IP100, IP200, IP300).

The second stage is analysis and prediction in Python. Results from each season are combined into a per-polygon panel. Planting dates are compared with the historical onset of the wet season from IMERG, and climate indices from ERA5 are tested as predictors.

Results and Current Limitations

The monitoring workflow now produces per-polygon outputs for 2015/16 through 2025/26, covering 57 polygons and about 500 usable polygon-season records after quality filtering. The data show clear two-cycle and three-cycle cropping patterns, with most polygons in MT1 and MT2.

On prediction, the project is candid about its limits. Leave-one-year-out validation shows that climate predictors (ENSO indices, the Indian Ocean Dipole, and rainfall) do not improve on historical averages, given the eleven planting seasons available for a single regency. The strongest predictor of planting date is each polygon’s own history: a per-polygon baseline achieves a mean absolute error of about 33 days, compared with about 48 days for a regency-wide average. The 2027 and 2028 planting ranges are therefore based on historical patterns, with 80 percent ranges derived from the observed error distribution, and are not presented as climate-driven forecasts.

Benefits

The system gives extension workers and farmer groups a per-field view of planting timing and cropping intensity, derived from open satellite data rather than field surveys. Flood-period detection can support early warning for planting decisions. Because all processing uses free data and open tools, the workflow can be repeated for other regencies and seasons with little additional cost.

Intended Impact

The goal is to support better planning of seed, fertilizer, and labor distribution, and to give local agricultural agencies a repeatable, evidence-based picture of rice cropping calendars. The project also establishes a method for evaluating forecasts honestly against baselines, which is useful for agencies deciding whether a predictive model is worth operational use.

Tools and Technologies

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript API) for satellite processing and export. Python with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, and openpyxl for data merging, validation, and reporting. Data sources include NASA HLS (Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2), NASA GPM IMERG V07, ECMWF ERA5 and ERA5-Land, NOAA OISST, and FAO GAUL administrative boundaries. Development ran on a standard Windows laptop with Anaconda, with all heavy computation executed in the cloud.

Creativity and Approach

Rather than predicting planting dates from climate alone, the project starts from what farmers actually do in each field and treats climate as a test of whether it adds value. The phenology algorithm avoids fixed thresholds by detecting peaks and troughs with an amplitude requirement, which makes it adaptable to different cropping patterns. The honest evaluation framework, which compares every model against a baseline and reports when none beats it, is a deliberate design choice.

Factors Considered

The team considered several factors when designing the pilot in Purworejo Regency, Central Java. The first was data availability. The HLS record provides usable Sentinel-2 and Landsat observations from 2015 onward, which limits the planting history to roughly [N] seasons. The team therefore treated the analysis as a short-record study and avoided long-term trend claims.

The second was cloud contamination in optical imagery. Cloud cover during the wet season removes many observations, and the team measured this directly by counting valid 15-day composites per polygon. In the sample output, one polygon had 22 of 24 periods with valid data, which shows that gaps are common but manageable. Polygons with fewer valid periods were excluded from the analysis, and gaps were filled only by carrying forward the previous valid value, so the method does not invent observations.

The third was the distinction between observed and predicted seasons. Planting dates for past seasons were derived from satellite observations, while planting dates for 2027 and 2028 are model outputs. The team kept these in separate files and labeled predictions explicitly, so that observed results are never presented as forecasts.

The fourth was overfitting. With only eleven seasons of planting history, a model with several climate predictors can fit the past well but perform poorly on new seasons. The team therefore compared every model against a historical baseline using leave-one-year-out validation. In this pilot, climate predictors such as ENSO, the Indian Ocean Dipole, and rainfall did not improve on a per-polygon baseline, and the team reported this result rather than adopting a more complex model.

The fifth was the need to avoid overstating certainty. The 80 percent prediction ranges for 2027 and 2028 are based on the observed error distribution from validation, not on confidence intervals from a statistical model. They describe the typical spread of planting dates, and the report states that they are not climate-driven forecasts.

The last factor was the difference between sample size and the number of polygons. Polygons within one season share the same rainfall onset and climate conditions, so they are not statistically independent. The effective sample for climate analysis is therefore the number of seasons, which is [N], not the [N] polygons multiplied by the number of seasons. The team reflected this in the validation design, which holds out entire seasons rather than individual polygons.
